content: The risk of snakebite is a daily concern for millions of people worldwide, particularly those engaged in routine activities such as walking to school, tending gardens, herding livestock, fetching water, or even using outdoor toilets. A single misstep, a brief lapse in attention, or being in the wrong place at the wrong time can result in a potentially fatal encounter. Snakebite envenoming is a neglected tropical disease (NTD) that causes significant suffering, disability, and premature death across all continents. Each year, there are an estimated 7 million cases of envenoming, resulting in 81,000 to 138,000 deaths. The economic burden of snakebite envenoming is immense, often unmanageable in lowand middle-income countries, where victims and their families, particularly in poor communities, lack access to social security systems. The financial strain frequently drives families deeper into poverty, trapping them in cycles of debt and undermining their futures. Children are especially vulnerable to snakebite envenoming, often suffering severe consequences such as disability or death. In homes where families are exposed to this threat, snakebites are a source of considerable fear and anxiety. In 2018, the 71st World Health Assembly adopted a comprehensive resolution calling for a coordinated global response to address the burden of snakebite envenoming. In response, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed a comprehensive strategy to reduce mortality and disability from snakebite envenoming by 50% by 2030. This strategy focuses on empowering countries, setting priorities, and aligning with WHO’s 13th General Programme of Work and the Sustainable Development Goals. The strategy emphasizes improving community education about snakebite risks, encouraging individuals to seek healthcare, and ensuring intensified case management for every patient. First aid, effective and affordable treatment provided by well-trained medical staff, and rehabilitation are critical components to help victims recover and return to productive lives. The strategy also aims to build a stable and sustainable market for safe, effective, and affordable antivenoms. This includes ensuring that antivenom production meets internationally accepted standards through collaboration among academia, industry, and public and private institutions. WHO plans to address the current antivenom supply crisis by creating a revolving stockpile of proven, effective antivenoms to ensure timely distribution to areas of need. Strengthening health systems is a core component of the strategy. This involves integrating snakebite prevention, treatment, and management into national health systems, plans, and policy frameworks. The WHO Health Systems Framework will guide these efforts to ensure more effective and sustainable solutions. The strategy also highlights the importance of partnerships, coordination, and resource mobilization. Advocacy will be essential to build a global coalition to drive change, generate investment, implement projects, and accelerate research into new therapies, diagnostics, and medical interventions. Country capacity-building and knowledge exchange will be prioritized to ensure locally relevant solutions. The strategy will be piloted in 10–12 high-burden countries between 2019 and 2020, with plans to scale up to 35–40 countries by 2024 as resources increase. By 2030, the strategy aims to be fully integrated into public health agendas worldwide. Regular reviews and adaptations will ensure the strategy remains effective and meets the needs of countries. Through advocacy and collaboration, WHO seeks to build a sustainable global coalition committed to achieving the target of halving the number of snakebite deaths and cases of disability by 2030. This will require transformational public–private investment and long-term commitment from governments and partners. The success of the program during its initial years will determine whether support can be secured for the full 12-year strategy. WHO will prepare a detailed work plan and an evidence-based investment case to demonstrate the cost-effectiveness and benefits of interventions, providing compelling arguments for investment, support, and participation. Countries are encouraged to mobilize domestic and international resources to achieve sustainable financing and implementation of their control programs, with strong technical support from WHO.
